newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Commonwealth officials start talks in Nigeria.
newsitem.headline: Commonwealth officials start talks in Nigeria.

text.p: A Commonwealth delegation began talks with Nigerian officials on Monday to press the military government to allow a probe into human rights and its progress towards returning to civilian rule.

The team of four officials, led by Commonwealth Deputy Secretary-General Srina Vasan, a former Indian ambassador to Nigeria and deputy foreign minister, went into a meeting behind closed doors in the capital, Abuja.
Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi, a vocal critic of the Commonwealth's decision to suspend Nigeria, said he had no plans to meet the officials himself.
"They have not asked to see me, and why should they? They are here to discuss with officials the modalities and dates for the ministerial level meeting," Ikimi told Reuters.
"This was set out in the letter which they sent explaining their mission,"

Commonwealth ministers, meeting in London last month, agreed to send the officials to pave the way for a ministerial level mission, after a proposed visit was called off when Nigeria imposed strict conditions.
The Commonwealth, concerned about human rights, wants to send a fact-finding team that would meet people outside the government, including the opposition and political prisoners.

But Abuja says the only question on the agenda was Nigeria's suspension from the Commonwealth of former British territories last November after the execution of nine rights activists including author Ken Saro-Wiwa.
"Our position on the mandate of the Commonwealth remains clear and has not changed," Ikimi said.
A Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG) was set up after the executions last November, which triggered worldwide condemnation of Nigeria's military government.

CMAG agreed in May to impose sanctions to push Nigeria toward democracy, including a ban on sporting links and arms sales. But at a meeting in London in June, CMAG said the measures would be suspended until a New York meeting in September to give Nigeria a chance for further talks.
Only Canada said it would go it alone and impose its own sanctions. It is pushing for other Commonwealth countries to take a harder line.
Nigeria on Friday said it was closing its embassy in Canada because of economic constraints.
Military ruler General Sani Abacha last year set out a plan to restore civilian rule by October 1998, which critics at home and abroad say takes too long.
The last attempt to end army rule collapsed in 1993, when a previous military government annulled elections and plunged Nigeria into political crisis.
